title: Manacher's Algorithm for Palindromes
summary: Manacher's algorithm finds every palindromic substring's radius in O(n), not O(n²), by unifying odd and even lengths with separators and reusing mirrored radii inside a known palindrome.

slides.markdown:
"Longest palindromic substring" is a staple interview question, and the naive approach — expand around every possible center — is O(n²). **Manacher's algorithm** computes the radius of the largest palindrome centered at *every* position in O(n), a full order of magnitude better.

The algorithm rests on two ideas: a unification trick that turns every palindrome, odd or even length, into an odd-length one via separators; and a mirror trick that reuses previously computed radii instead of re-expanding from scratch. Neither idea alone is exotic — the combination is what gets you to linear time.

slides.sectionTitle: The O(n²) baseline: expand around center
slides.markdown:
The direct approach: for every possible center (n of them for odd-length palindromes, n-1 gaps between characters for even-length ones), expand outward while the characters on both sides match, tracking the largest radius found.

This is correct and O(n²) in the worst case — a string of all the same character (`"aaaa...a"`) forces every center's expansion to run nearly the full length of the string. It's also the algorithm every interviewer expects you to name first, since Manacher's only earns its complexity by comparison to this baseline.

slides.sectionTitle: Odd and even lengths as separate cases
slides.markdown:
A palindrome like `"aba"` has one center character; a palindrome like `"abba"` has a center between two characters — no single index is the middle. Handling these as genuinely separate code paths (one loop expanding from a character, another expanding from a gap) is exactly what most naive implementations do, and it works, but it doubles the bookkeeping and is the first thing that gets bug-prone under interview pressure — an off-by-one in the even-length branch that doesn't show up in your odd-length test cases.

Manacher's algorithm's entire opening move is refusing to keep these separate.

Insert a separator character (one that never appears in the input, e.g. `'#'`) between every character and at both ends. `"abba"` becomes `"#a#b#b#a#"`; `"aba"` becomes `"#a#b#a#"`.

Now **every** palindrome in the transformed string is odd-length, centered on a real character. A center on an original character corresponds to an odd-length palindrome in the original string; a center on a separator corresponds to an even-length one. This single transformation is why Manacher's never needs a separate even-length code path — one algorithm, one loop, handles both cases uniformly, because they've become the same shape.

Suppose you've found a palindrome centered at `c` spanning `[l, r]`, and you're now computing the radius at some position `i` inside that span. Because everything inside `[l, r]` is itself a palindrome (mirrored around `c`), position `i`'s mirror image `i' = 2c - i` has *already* had its radius computed — and by the symmetry of the outer palindrome, `i`'s radius starts out knowing at least as much as `i'`'s radius, up to the boundary of `[l, r]`.

This is the same reuse principle as KMP's LPS fallback and the Z-array's Z-box: don't recompute information the algorithm has already proven, only extend past what's already known.

slides.sectionTitle: The radius array and the rightmost boundary
slides.markdown:
![The transformed string with its radius array below, a bracket over the current rightmost palindrome span, and a mirror arrow between positions sharing that radius](assets/manachers-radius-boundary.svg)

As the scan proceeds left to right, `[l, r]` only ever grows to track the rightmost-reaching palindrome discovered so far — exactly the same bookkeeping shape as the Z-array's Z-box, applied to palindrome radii instead of prefix matches.

slides.sectionTitle: Computing the radius array in one linear pass
slides.markdown:
```python
def manacher(s):
    t = '#' + '#'.join(s) + '#'
    n = len(t)
    radius = [0] * n
    center = right = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if i < right:
            mirror = 2 * center - i
            radius[i] = min(right - i, radius[mirror])   # cap at the known boundary
        while (i - radius[i] - 1 >= 0 and i + radius[i] + 1 < n
               and t[i - radius[i] - 1] == t[i + radius[i] + 1]):
            radius[i] += 1                                 # expand past what's proven
        if i + radius[i] > right:
            center, right = i, i + radius[i]
    return radius, t
```

The capped starting value — `min(right - i, radius[mirror])` — is the same style of safe-lower-bound trick the Z-array uses: never assume more than what's proven not to cross the current known boundary, then let the `while` loop verify anything beyond it with direct comparison.

slides.sectionTitle: Forgetting to cap the mirrored radius
slides.markdown:
The single most common Manacher's bug: setting `radius[i] = radius[mirror]` directly, without capping it at `right - i`. This breaks the moment the mirrored palindrome would extend past the current known boundary `right` — you'd be assuming information about characters the algorithm hasn't actually verified yet.

Concretely: if the mirror position's palindrome happens to be unusually long and pokes outside `[l, r]`, you can't trust that its full extent mirrors correctly, because the symmetry guarantee only holds *inside* the known palindrome `[l, r]`. Capping at `right - i` is what forces the subsequent `while` loop to actually verify anything beyond the proven region instead of blindly trusting an unverified mirror value.

Once the radius array is built, the longest palindromic substring is found by taking the maximum radius value, say at index `i` with radius `r`. In the transformed string with separators, that radius directly gives the length of the palindrome in the **original** string: the original-string length equals `r` (the separator positions cancel out algebraically), and the original starting index is `(i - r) // 2`.

Getting the index math right here — converting from the separator-padded coordinate system back to the original string — is a common place to lose a few minutes in an interview; work it out on a short example (`"aba"` → `"#a#b#a#"`) before trusting the formula under pressure.

| | Expand around center | Manacher's |
|---|---|---|
| Time | O(n²) worst case | O(n) guaranteed |
| Code complexity | Simple, two cases (odd/even) | More bookkeeping (separators, mirror, boundary cap) |
| When it's worth it | n is small, or you just need *a* correct answer quickly | n is large, or the problem explicitly wants the optimal bound |

In a live interview, many candidates are better served starting with expand-around-center — it's correct, it's fast to write, and it demonstrates the core palindrome intuition — then naming Manacher's as the O(n) follow-up if asked to optimize further. Reaching straight for Manacher's when the input is small is over-engineering the same way a hash map is overkill for a 5-element lookup.
